items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Lester Young composed a melody over ‘I Got Rhythm’ and he called it ‘Lester Leaps In.’

ctx.x: You ever have any train wrecks?

Oh, big ones man. The one that I can think of offhand that comes to me, it’s funny and it was a real learning experience for me. I got put with a quartet. Piano, bass, drums and an alto player, to do a festival. An indoor festival. And everything was going fine. We were about 3/4 of the way through the set. And it’s like this it’s bass, drums, alto, piano. And I turned to the band and I say, “rhythm changes in E flat.” Then I turned to the audience © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

and say, “George and Ira Gershwin wrote a song called ‘I Got Rhythm.’ Lester Young composed a melody over ‘I Got Rhythm’ and he called it ‘Lester Leaps In.’ The lyrical version is called ‘I Got the Blues.’” I turned to the band and say, “one/two/one-two-three- four.” Now maybe they weren’t listening. But the bass player — you know where this is going already, right? The bass player and the drummer start to play rhythm changes. And the piano player and the alto player are playing the blues. Now that works for…

items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Well I’m a fan of Lester Young and his lingo... They were, to me, they were funny and bright and articulate and they said a lot with a little.

ctx.x: Yeah. A very long time ago I got to sit in with Lou Donaldson because the bass player that I knew was playing with Lou. And he said, “Hey man, let this cat sit in.” This was a long time ago. And Lou at first didn’t know me, why would he have me sit in? And the bass player kept making it — and I’m like, “Please leave Lou alone.” And he finally did bring me up. And I know that Lou plays a lot of Charlie Parker. So I said, “Can we do ‘Lady Be Good’?” And I sang “Lady Be Good,” and then Lou played a solo, and then I…

“Well, for me that’s one of Charlie Parker’s most well-constructed solos. And then here’s the punch line. He said, “But he had to play something, because he was standing next to Lester Young.” So that put the whole thing into context for me. Not only was it a great solo, but I didn’t know that when he played that solo it was at Jazz at the Philharmonic and Prez was on the gig. And Charlie Parker was very young at the time, or relatively young, and he knew that he was going to be playing with his idol, Lester…
